hook.prompt: On the road to agenda-setting theory, what does Lippmann’s island story show?
options: That the news media often lie on purpose
That how often the mail steamer arrives determines public opinion
That people get to know the distant world through simplified pictures received from others, and act accordingly
That newspaper readers do not like war news
hook.explain: The right answer is the third option: the islanders acted wrongly because the picture in their heads had gone out of date. Do not fall for the lying trap: Lippmann says “By fictions I do not mean lies”, meaning that people get to know their environment through representations they build themselves; so the problem is not bad faith but the fact that reality is too big to know directly. The mail steamer is a detail of the story, not its main idea.

cohen-line.prompt: For a whole week a newspaper covers only city water cuts on its front page, and says nothing at all about who is responsible for them. According to Cohen’s sentence, what does the newspaper give its reader?
options: A view on who the culprit is (what to think)
The impression that water cuts are an issue worth dwelling on (what to think about)
A negative attitude towards the mayor
Nothing; according to Cohen, the newspaper does not influence its reader
cohen-line.explain: Cohen separates choosing issues from voicing opinions. The newspaper voices no opinion, but by pushing the issue forward insistently it signals “this is important”; that is the second option. The first and third options slide towards the “what to think” side, that is, towards what the theory does not claim. The fourth option misreads Cohen’s sentence: Cohen is not saying the media are powerless, but that their power lies elsewhere.

people-time.prompt: Match each name with the contribution most associated with them.
pairs: Walter Lippmann
The idea of “the pictures in our heads” and the pseudo-environment (1922)
Bernard Cohen
The line about the press’s success at telling us “what to think about” (1963)
McCombs and Shaw
The Chapel Hill study of the 1968 election
Iyengar, Peters and Kinder
Experiments showing the effect of television news on perceived importance (1982)
people-time.explain: The most common mistake is to count Lippmann or Cohen as the founder of the theory. Both prepared the ground of ideas; it was McCombs and Shaw who measured it and named the theory. Another mix-up is in the dates: the experiments date from about fourteen years after Chapel Hill (1982).

claim.prompt: Complete the sentence with Cohen’s distinction.
claim.text: In the language of the theory, the news media are successful not in telling people {{1}}, but in telling them {{2}}.

options: what to think about
what to think
what to think about
which channel to watch

claim.explain: The heart of the theory is Cohen’s distinction: by pushing issues forward, the media steer what people think about; dictating what they should think is not the theory’s claim. Swapping the two phrases is the trap most often fallen into in exams.

myth-what-to-think.prompt: Agenda-setting theory argues that the media can easily reverse people’s attitudes on an issue.
myth-what-to-think.explain: False. The theory’s core claim is not the reversal of attitudes but the transfer of the order of importance of issues; the 1972 article even states plainly that the media may have little effect on the direction and intensity of attitudes. The trap is to confuse the theory with the “media brainwash” view; the historical home of that view is the hypodermic needle (magic bullet) model.

agendas-three.prompt: A researcher counts, by issue, the front-page headlines of three national newspapers in March; then she ranks the answers to “What do you think is the most important problem facing the country?” in a survey of a thousand people and compares the two lists. Which two agendas has she compared?
options: The media agenda and the public agenda
The public agenda and the policy agenda
The policy agenda and the media agenda
Only the media agenda; the survey has nothing to do with the agenda
agendas-three.explain: The headlines represent the media agenda and the survey answers the public agenda; the right answer is the first option. To measure the policy agenda one would have had to look at the priorities of parliament or the government (bills, budget decisions and the like); that is why the second and third options are wrong. The last option overlooks that the public agenda is measured by survey.

related-terms.prompt: Match each concept with its best-fitting definition.
pairs: First-level agenda-setting
Which issues are seen as important?
Second-level agenda-setting
Which attributes of the issue or candidate stand out?
Priming
The prominent issue becomes the yardstick in judging a leader
Gatekeeping
The process of choosing which story gets on air and which does not
related-terms.explain: A short way to keep the distinction in mind: the first level is what is important, the second level is which side of the issue is important, priming is by what you decide, and gatekeeping is who selects the story. In exams, the first level, the second level and priming are the trio most often mixed up.

assumptions.prompt: Agenda-setting theory assumes that the news media reflect the real world one to one; what the theory calls the “agenda” is this reflection.
assumptions.explain: False. The theory assumes just the opposite: the media are a flawed map of reality, and what matters is which regions of that map are drawn thick. Funkhouser’s 1960s finding supports this: press and public interest had come apart from real-world indicators. If the media reflected reality one to one, there would be no need for a separate theory called agenda-setting; the fit between the media and the public would be explained as “reaction to the same reality”.

steps-mechanism.prompt: Put the agenda’s journey in the right order.
items: Material reaches the newsroom from events, sources and other media
Editors select, rank and foreground stories
The audience infers the issue’s importance from cues of space, time and repetition
The order of issues on the public agenda moves closer to the media agenda
The prominent issue becomes a yardstick for judging leaders (priming)
steps-mechanism.explain: The chain of logic: first the material, then selection and ranking, then the audience reading the cue, then the shift of the public agenda, and last the consequences. The most common mistake is to put priming (the final consequence) before the shift of the public agenda: priming requires that the issue first become salient, that is, that the agenda transfer take place.

nfo.prompt: Which of the three imaginary people above would be expected to have the agenda most similar to the news agenda?
options: Berk, because he watches no news, so his agenda is unaffected by the media
Ceren, because she is very interested in the election and therefore trusts the media most
Ayşe, because both her interest and her uncertainty are high, that is, she has the highest need for orientation
All three equally, because the theory works the same for everyone
nfo.explain: In Ayşe, relevance and uncertainty are both high: she has the highest need for orientation, the person in whom the media’s agenda-setting effect is expected to be strongest. Ceren is interested but decided; since her uncertainty is low, her need for orientation is only moderate. Berk’s interest is low, so his need for orientation is low. The last option misses that the theory is conditional, not “the same for everyone”.

chapel-hill.prompt: Why did the researchers take only voters who had not yet decided into the sample?
options: Because decided voters refused to take part in the survey
Because it had earlier been proven that undecided voters follow the media the most
Because the number of undecided voters in the town was very small
Because undecided voters were assumed to be the people most open and most susceptible to campaign information
chapel-hill.explain: The article states the rationale plainly: the undecided were chosen because they were assumed to be the people most open or most susceptible to campaign information. The other options are made-up reasons that do not appear in the article. This choice has a cost too: the sample does not represent all voters; you will see this again on the critique card.

chapel-hill-results.prompt: If selective perception were correct, what would we expect to see in the Chapel Hill data?
options: Voters’ ranking giving its highest correlation with the composite of all the news
Voters’ ranking giving its highest correlation with the news most about their own candidate
No correlation at all between voters’ ranking and the news
Undecided voters not differing from decided voters
chapel-hill-results.explain: Selective perception means people looking more at the news that belongs to their own side; in that case the rankings would overlap most with that news: the second option. The first option is exactly what was found (18 of 24 comparisons) and supports the agenda-setting interpretation. The third option would be the result not of selective perception but of the media having no influence at all; the fourth option is unrelated to this test.

later-work.prompt: In terms of the assumption that “the media reflect reality as it is”, what did Funkhouser’s study of the 1960s show?
options: Press coverage matched real-world indicators exactly
Public opinion moved completely independently of the press
Television was stronger than newspapers on every issue
Press coverage and public interest moved together, but both diverged from real-world indicators
later-work.explain: According to Funkhouser, the press and public opinion moved together but neither was in line with real-world indicators (for Vietnam, campus unrest and urban riots, interest peaked a year or two before the actual conditions). The first option is the exact opposite; the second option denies that the media and public opinion moved together; the third option reverses the television–newspaper comparison (the Charlotte finding that the newspaper came first).

causal-direction.prompt: Which of the following most strongly supports the claim that “the news set the public agenda” in terms of causality?
options: Randomly dividing participants into groups, having one group watch news that emphasises a certain issue, then comparing perceived importance between the groups
Finding a high correlation between the news ranking and the survey ranking in an election week
Asking newspaper readers “which issue do you find important?”
Comparing two newspapers’ headlines
causal-direction.explain: Random assignment and controlled exposure is the only design that rules out direction and third variables, as in Iyengar, Peters and Kinder’s experiments. A high correlation (like Chapel Hill’s +0.967) shows a relationship but not its direction; this is the most tempting wrong option. A survey question measures only the public agenda, and a comparison of headlines only media agendas: neither can establish cause and effect.

critique-design.prompt: A friend says “McCombs and Shaw proved in 1972 that the media set the agenda.” Which is the most accurate correction?
options: He is right; the 0.967 correlation proves causality.
Wrong; because the study covered only decided voters.
The authors themselves wrote that the correlations do not prove agenda-setting and present a picture consistent with the theory.
Wrong; because no correlation was computed in the article at all.
critique-design.explain: The article’s discussion section says that the agenda-setting function is not proved by these correlations, but that the evidence is consistent with the conditions that should be found if agenda-setting were at work: the third option. The first option confuses correlation with causation; the second misreports the sample (there were undecided voters); the fourth ignores the article’s main result (+0.967 and +0.979).

critique-lab.prompt: Which observation most weakens the explanation “only real prices drive both the headlines and public worry”?
options: Inflation headlines and public worry rose together within the same month.
Most people in the poll said they felt the price rises when shopping for groceries.
Newspapers gave inflation only the back pages.
During a period when prices stayed constant, public worry rose a few weeks after a newspaper group started reporting on inflation.
critique-lab.explain: If coverage changes while prices are constant and worry then rises, the “only real prices” explanation (the third variable) weakens and the time order supports agenda-setting: the fourth option. The first option fits all three explanations, so it does not discriminate. The second option strengthens the real-world cue; the third option is not directly related to the issue.

today-networks.prompt: A commentator says “Twitter’s agenda runs the newspapers all by itself.” What does the finding of Neuman and colleagues on 29 issues in 2012 say against this claim?
options: It shows that social media have wiped out traditional media’s agenda-setting power entirely.
It shows that the traditional and social media agendas are related but that their rhythms differ significantly; the influence is not one-way.
It shows that social media operate wholly independently of traditional media.
It shows that the Twitter agenda is always set by the newspapers.
today-networks.explain: Neuman and colleagues did not find a one-way model; the agendas were related but moved to different rhythms: the second option. The commentator’s claim is a one-way claim saying “Twitter runs the newspapers”; the fourth option says the opposite but makes the same mistake, one-directionality. The first and third options are also over-readings: there was a relation between the agendas; traditional media neither lost their influence nor turned out to be wholly independent of social media.

today-trending.prompt: In Kwak and colleagues’ 2009 data, most of Twitter’s trending topics consisted of everyday private chat and personal posts.
today-trending.explain: False. More than 85% of the trending topics were headline news or persistent news; that is, what we call “the public’s own agenda” largely reflected the news agenda. The trap is to think that social media produce an agenda independent of the news. But it is not a lasting conclusion either: this 2009 data cannot be taken as directly valid for today’s algorithmic feeds.

turkey-studies.prompt: What was the main difference of the Hazar and Sbouh (2020) study from the classic agenda-setting design?
options: It measured the media agenda by participants’ perception, not by content analysis
It measured the public agenda by observation, not by a survey
It examined only television news
It sampled only undecided voters
turkey-studies.explain: The classic approach (like Chapel Hill) first analyses media content and then compares it with the public agenda; this study measured the media agenda through students’ perception, and the authors point this out themselves. The other options are not in the study’s design: the public agenda was measured by survey, the sample was students, not voters, and it was not only television that was looked at.

exam-patterns.prompt: An exam question asks “which is correct?” about McCombs and Shaw’s Chapel Hill study. Which option is correct?
options: It was done in 1968 with 1,000 decided voters and was based on Lippmann’s data.
It was done in New York in 1972 and examined television news.
In autumn 1968, 100 undecided voters were interviewed; the article was published in 1972.
It was an experimental study; participants were made to watch different news.
exam-patterns.explain: The interviews were carried out between 18 September and 6 October 1968 with 100 undecided voters; the article was published in 1972: the third option. The first option enlarges the sample, changes the voter type and makes Lippmann a data source (Lippmann is a 1922 author). The second option mixes up place, year and medium type. The fourth option confuses a survey-and-content-analysis study with Iyengar and colleagues’ experiments of 1982.

summary.text: In the 1968 Chapel Hill study of {{1}} undecided voters, the correlation for major news items was +{{2}}.
summary.explain: The number of interviews was 100; 45 was the size of the subgroup leaning towards a candidate (used in the selective-perception test). The correlation for major news was +0.967 and for minor news +0.979. Mixing up 100 and 45, and the two correlations, is a typical exam error.

quiz.prompt: Which of the following best summarises the basic claim of agenda-setting theory?
options: The media quickly reverse an audience’s view on an issue.
The media only reinforce views the audience already holds.
The emphasis the media give to issues influences how important the audience considers those issues.
The media determine which channel the audience watches.
quiz.explain: The theory says the order of importance of issues in the media is transferred to the public’s order of importance: the third option. The first option is the “strong effects / brainwashing” view, not the theory’s claim. The second option belongs to the “reinforcement” approach, that is, to the limited-effects tradition. The fourth is about the audience’s channel choice and is unrelated to the theory.

quiz.prompt: In their 1972 article, McCombs and Shaw wrote that the +0.967 correlation proved that the media set the agenda.
quiz.explain: False. The authors wrote that the agenda-setting function is not proved by these correlations, but that the evidence is consistent with the conditions that should be found if agenda-setting were at work. They also noted that aggregate units were compared and that the next step should be the individual level. The trap is to count a high correlation automatically as causality.

quiz.prompt: Match each study with its main finding.
pairs: Funkhouser (1973)
Press and public interest moved together but diverged from real-world indicators
Winter and Eyal (1981)
On civil rights the best effect span was four to six weeks before the survey
Behr and Iyengar (1985)
Television news influenced public concern, not the other way round
Iyengar, Peters and Kinder (1982)
In experiments, television news changed perceived importance and the yardsticks for judging the president
Demers and colleagues (1989)
No support was found for the “obtrusiveness” hypothesis
quiz.explain: These five studies represent the “wave of testing” that came after the theory’s first evidence: the reality check (Funkhouser), time lag (Winter–Eyal), direction and real-world cues (Behr–Iyengar), experiment (Iyengar and colleagues), issue type (Demers and colleagues). The most often confused pair is time lag and the question of direction: Winter–Eyal studied the span, Behr–Iyengar the direction.

quiz.prompt: Put the following in order from oldest to newest.
items: Cohen, The Press and Foreign Policy
The Chapel Hill interviews and media content coding
The second-level agenda-setting study in the Spanish elections
quiz.explain: The order: 1922, 1963, 1968, 1973, 1982, 1997. The most common mistake is to put Chapel Hill at 1972: 1972 is the year the article was published; the data were collected in autumn 1968. The second trap is to put Funkhouser (1973) before Chapel Hill.

quiz.prompt: Complete the definition of need for orientation.
quiz.text: Need for orientation combines a person’s {{1}} regarding an issue with their level of {{2}} about it; when both are high, the media’s agenda-setting effect is expected to be {{3}}.

options: educational level
personal relevance
age
certainty
income
uncertainty
weaker
stronger
the same

quiz.explain: McCombs and Weaver’s concept has two components: personal relevance and uncertainty. If interest and indecision are both high, the person needs a “map” the most and leans more on the media’s ranking. The trap is to count a person high in certainty (the opposite of uncertainty) as open to influence too: in a decided person, need for orientation is at most moderate.

quiz.scenario: Imagine: for a month the local newspaper of a fictional town called Kumsalköy gives equal and prominent space to two issues: (A) the water cuts in the neighbourhoods and (B) a government crisis in a faraway country. In a survey at the end of the month, Kumsalköy residents rank B high among “the most important issues”. A researcher wants to attribute this to agenda-setting.

parts.prompt: Which alternative explanation should the researcher consider before attributing the result to agenda-setting?
options: That the crisis had in any case found wide resonance in the international press and other channels; that is, a common cause outside the news.
That the newspaper ran the B stories on the front page.
That the survey was conducted in Kumsalköy.
That the newspaper also covered the A stories.
parts.explain: Before advancing agenda-setting, third variables have to be ruled out (here: a big crisis being talked about everywhere); this is why the “real-world cues”, from Funkhouser to Behr and Iyengar, matter. The second option is the very mechanism to be explained, not an alternative. The third and fourth options do not explain the result.

parts.prompt: According to Zucker’s “variable media effect” hypothesis, on which issue would the effect of the news be expected to be greater?
options: A, because Kumsalköy residents live the water cuts directly
B, because people do not experience it directly and learn about it only from the news
Equal; the hypothesis does not take issue type into account
Neither; the hypothesis applies only to television
parts.explain: According to Zucker, the less directly an issue is experienced, the greater the effect of the news: B. Since A is an issue lived directly (obtrusive), the effect would be expected to be smaller. But this hypothesis is disputed: in 1989 Demers and colleagues could not find support for this “obtrusiveness” hypothesis.

parts.prompt: Whose agenda in the survey would be expected to be the most similar to the newspaper’s agenda?
options: Someone who does not care about the crisis at all
Someone who is interested in the crisis and has long since decided whom to support
Someone who never reads the newspaper
Someone who is interested in the crisis but does not know whose side to take
parts.explain: In a person for whom relevance and uncertainty are both high, need for orientation is the highest and the media’s agenda effect is expected to be the strongest. In a decided, interested person uncertainty is low, so it is moderate; a person who is uninterested or never reads the paper is not affected, because they are not exposed to the media or do not turn to it.

quiz.takeaway: Before attributing a match to agenda-setting, look at three things: (1) rule out common causes (real-world cues), (2) issue type, (3) who would be affected more. The theory says not “always, in everyone” but “under these conditions, in these people”.

quiz.prompt: Before an election, economic news moves to the top and voters give more weight to economic performance than before when judging a candidate. Which concept does this exemplify?
options: Gatekeeping
Cultivation
The spiral of silence
Priming
quiz.explain: A prominent issue becoming the yardstick for judging a leader is priming (as seen in the evaluations of Reagan after Iran–Contra). Gatekeeping is about the selection of stories, cultivation about long-term television exposure, and the spiral of silence about the fear of being left in the minority; none of them explains this scenario.

quiz.prompt: What was the real advantage of the 1972 Charlotte panel study over the single-town Chapel Hill cross-section?
options: That it included only decided voters
That, by following the same voters over time, it could look at the cause–effect order
That it focused only on television
That it covered more media organisations
quiz.explain: A panel design follows the same people over several waves; so one can look at whether the media agenda predicts the later public agenda (time order). Chapel Hill was a single cross-section. The other options are not Charlotte’s advantage: both television and newspapers were examined in Charlotte; the difference lay not in the number of media or the type of voter but in the time dimension.

quiz.prompt: In Kwak and colleagues’ 2009 Twitter data, more than 85% of trending topics were headline news or persistent news.
quiz.explain: True. The authors classified 4,262 trending topics and found that most of them (more than 85%) were headline news or persistent news. This shows that the social media agenda was largely tied to the news agenda; but since it is a snapshot of 2009, it cannot be carried directly over to today’s algorithmic feeds.

quiz.prompt: What answer did Barberá and colleagues’ Twitter study of the 113th US Congress give to the question “who follows whom?”
options: Legislators largely set the public’s agenda.
The public talks completely independently of legislators.
Legislators follow the public’s issues rather than steering them; what is more, they are more responsive to their own supporters than to the general public.
Only traditional media set the issues.
quiz.explain: The finding: legislators follow the public’s issues rather than steering them, and this result does not change even when the media’s agenda-setting effects are controlled for; they are also more responsive to their supporters than to the general public. The first option is the exact opposite. The second and fourth options ignore the reciprocal relation the study showed.

quiz.prompt: Match each concept with the imaginary example that fits it.
pairs: First-level agenda-setting
Newspapers giving a lot of space to the economy and the public starting to see the economy as the most important issue
Second-level agenda-setting
A candidate being constantly presented as “experienced” in the news and voters finding him experienced
Priming
As security news increases, security performance gaining weight in the evaluation of the leader
Intermedia agenda-setting
A newspaper’s headline issue also standing out in television news the following week
Need for orientation
A voter who is interested in the issue but cannot decide turning more to the news media
quiz.explain: Each example answers a different question: which issue (first level), which attribute of the issue (second level), by which yardstick the decision is made (priming), who influences the media agenda (intermedia), who is affected more (need for orientation). The most often confused pair is the second level and priming: the former changes the perception of an object’s attribute, the latter the yardstick of evaluation.

quiz.prompt: According to Walgrave and Van Aelst (2006), which is true of the media’s power over the policy agenda?
options: This power is conditional: it depends on issue type, medium, the form of the story and the political context.
Whatever the media publish, politicians immediately put that issue on their agenda.
The media have no influence on the policy agenda whatsoever.
Only television influences the policy agenda.
quiz.explain: The authors argue that the media’s influence on the policy agenda depends on a set of conditions (input variables: issue type, medium, story type; at the centre the political context) and that outcomes range from “no adoption” to “fast and real adoption”. The second option assumes an automatic effect, the third denies the effect entirely; there is no finding supporting the fourth option.

quiz.prompt: To stress that the media are a flawed representation of reality, which concept from Lippmann did McCombs and Shaw use in their 1972 article?
options: Two-step flow
The spiral of silence
The gatekeeper
The pseudo-environment
quiz.explain: The article writes that the “pseudo-environment” the media reflect is not a perfect representation of the real campaign; the concept comes from Lippmann’s 1922 book. Two-step flow is Lazarsfeld and Katz’s, the spiral of silence is Noelle-Neumann’s, and gatekeeping is the concept of a research tradition that began with White’s 1950 news-selection study; none of them is Lippmann’s concept.
